title: An ionic clock qubit inside a circular Rydberg atom
authors: Fabian Thielemann, Aaron Götzelmann, Marius Thomas, Einius Pultinevicius, Armin Humić, Christian Hölzl, Florian Meinert
abstract: Neutral atoms trapped in optical tweezers and excited to Rydberg states, together with trapped ions, are among the most advanced platforms for quantum simulation and quantum computing. Current experiments often rely on additional atoms in neighboring traps to encode ancilla qubits for local manipulation and readout. Here, we demonstrate a dual ion-Rydberg system comprising two qubits encoded in two individually controlled electrons of the same alkaline-earth atom. The first, a microwave qubit, is encoded in a pair of circular Rydberg states, while the second, an optical qubit, is encoded on a narrow quadrupole transition of the Rydberg atom's ionic core. We demonstrate coherent control of the optical qubit and achieve coherence times of several hundred microseconds under dynamical decoupling. Furthermore, we realize coherent coupling between the two electrons via electrostatic quadrupole interactions over the large separation between the Rydberg electron and the ionic core, and map out its angular tunability. Finally, we demonstrate a two-qubit operation, reminiscent of a Mølmer-Sørensen gate, that evolves through an entangled state of the two qubits driven by the quadrupole coupling. Our work opens a pathway to exploit a pair of individually controlled electronic qubits with tunable coupling for quantum simulation and quantum metrology.
summary: The paper reports on the realization and characterization of a novel dual qubit system using two distinct electronic transitions within a single alkaline-earth atom. By demonstrating coherent control, tunable coupling via quadrupole interactions, and executing a two-qubit gate, the work establishes a powerful platform for quantum simulation and metrology applications.
main_problem: To demonstrate a dual ion-Rydberg system within a single alkaline-earth atom capable of hosting two individually controlled electronic qubits for quantum simulation and metrology.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated coherent control, tunable coupling via electrostatic quadrupole interactions, and implemented a two-qubit gate operation analogous to a Mølmer-Sørensen gate using the coupled system.
method: Coherent microwave and optical spectroscopy, dynamical decoupling sequences (spin-echo, XY8), and state-selective field ionization detection were employed to characterize qubit coherence and coupling.
model_or_system: The platform uses a single strontium atom trapped in optical tweezers, encoding one qubit in circular Rydberg states (microwave) and the second in the narrow quadrupole transition of the ionic core (optical).
key_observables:
Coherence times ($T_2$ up to 550 $\mu$s), differential quadrupole shift ($\Delta
u_Q = 5.83 	ext{ kHz}$), and fidelity of two-qubit gate operations.
important_parameters: Electric field strengths ($|E|$ up to $3 	ext{ V/cm}$), Rydberg principal quantum number (e.g., $n=79, 81$), and coupling strength derived from quadrupole interactions.
main_assumptions: The ability to use the platform relies on the negligible autoionization rate of circular Rydberg states due to minimal wavefunction overlap with low-lying core orbitals.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the level schemes for both qubits, detection using state-dependent arrival time histograms (four basis states), spectroscopic measurements showing polarization dependence, and visualizations of gate operations like Husimi-Q distributions during XY8 sequences.
paper_structure: The work progresses by first establishing coherent control over individual qubits, then characterizing the tunable electrostatic quadrupole coupling between them, and finally demonstrating a full two-qubit quantum gate sequence using this coupled system.
why_interesting: This represents a significant advancement in solid-state/atomic quantum simulation platforms by integrating multiple types of highly controllable electronic degrees of freedom (microwave Rydberg vs. optical core transition) into one addressable unit.

(a) We excite one of the two valence electrons of 88Sr to the circular Rydberg state |79C⟩(yellow). A two-photon microwave transition to the |81C⟩state allows us to coherently control the state of the Rydberg qubit. We use a pair of push and repump beams to rapidly scatter photons on the ionic core D1 transition. Our clock laser, propagating orthogonal to the magnetic field B, excites the ionic core to the D5/2 state (colors used for the different beams match those used in b).
